vignette:
Arthur is a sixty-seven-year-old man, originally from a small island nation in Oceania, who has been living alone in a two-bedroom apartment in a quiet seaside town for the last five years, since his wife, Leilani, passed away. He came to therapy at the gentle insistence of his daughter, who lives in another state and worries about the way he has withdrawn from the world. He is a tall man, still with a strong frame, but he moves carefully, as if the air around him is fragile. He is an interior designer, a career he built over forty years, and he still takes on the occasional project for old clients. But lately, he says, he can no longer look at a room without seeing its exits.

The story he tells begins not in a therapist’s office, but on a cargo ship thirty-two years ago. Arthur was thirty-five, working as a design consultant for a hotel chain, and he had accepted a short contract to oversee the renovation of a resort on a remote island chain. He took a small cargo vessel to reach the site. The ship was intercepted by a group of men who held him and five other passengers in the hull for seventeen days. They were kept in a dark, windowless compartment that smelled of diesel and rust. He was tied to a metal pipe for most of that time. He does not describe the violence in detail, only that it was present, constant, and that the men who held him spoke a language he did not understand. He remembers the sound of the engine vibrating through the floor, the way the light never changed, and the certainty, after about the fifth day, that he would die there.

He was released in a negotiated exchange. He flew home, saw a doctor for his physical injuries, and never spoke of it again. He returned to work within a month. He married Leilani a year later. He designed beautiful, open, airy rooms for wealthy clients, full of natural light and soft textures. He thought he had moved on.

Now, thirty-two years later, Arthur cannot sit with his back to a door. He will not enter a room that does not have a window he can reach. His current project is a beach house for a retired couple, and he finds himself sketching escape routes instead of furniture layouts. He has stopped taking jobs that require him to be in a building without a clear, immediate path to the outside. He wakes at three in the morning with his heart pounding, convinced he can hear the low hum of a ship’s engine. He says the sound is so real that he has to walk through his apartment, touching the walls, to remind himself he is in a home. He has not slept through the night in over a year.

He stopped driving six months ago, after he became trapped in a traffic jam on a bridge. He says he felt the panic rise not from the height, but from the fact that he could not move, that he was contained, that the metal box of his car was a cell. He pulled over, abandoned the car on the shoulder, and walked home along the beach. He now takes the bus, but only on routes where he can sit near the rear exit. He avoids elevators. He avoids windowless conference rooms. He has told no one about these rules, not even his daughter. He calls them “preferences.”

The most difficult part, Arthur says, is that he no longer feels like a designer. He used to love the way light moved across a room. Now he looks at a space and sees only its constraints. He sees how easily a door could be blocked. He sees how a beautiful, tall window is just a way out. He has not told his clients this. He has not told anyone. He comes to therapy because his daughter is worried, but also because he is tired of measuring the distance to every door.
